title: The Weather Station - Breaking and Entering
transcript:
Tamara Lindeman of The Weather Station joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studios on 10 May 2018 to discuss her self-titled fourth album, songwriting and collaboration. She was in Melbourne for a Northcote Social Club show and dates supporting Marlon Williams, and performed ‘Free’ live in the studio. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: You started The Weather Station back, I believe, in 2006. The debut album, The Line, came out in 2009, and the self-titled album which Lauren just mentioned came out last year and was your fourth. Your music has poetic, literary lyrics with orchestral, folk and rock arrangements, but the project began on MySpace. You chose the name The Weather Station because your bio described you living in an abandoned Arctic weather station, and you were making atmospheric instrumental arrangements. How did the music evolve into more vocal and lyrical work?

Tamara: I think it just began based on my limitations. When I started making music, I couldn’t really play any instruments all that well. I could sing, but I’d never written a song. I just had this very strong compulsion to make music. I got some software from a friend and I started recording on my computer, and I made these atmospheric soundscapes because I had never picked up a guitar and written a song. I didn’t even play guitar at the time. I named it The Weather Station because I didn’t know other musicians. I wasn’t really a musician yet, but I wanted to put it on the internet and I just wanted some anonymity. So I pretended that it was these found recordings from this person. I was 20. Over time I became more and more interested, I think because that’s where I began, in a song that you can play anywhere at any time and it works. Something strong enough lyrically and melodically that it just stands up. I got into classic songwriting and I wanted to do that.

Simon: You grew up in rural Canada, spending quite a lot of time on your own. Apparently you would sing by yourself in the woods. Is that right?

Tamara: Yeah, totally. I always sang to myself and I always found it really soothing, actually. Because I grew up in the woods, nobody could hear me, so it was fine.

Simon: Would that have been a formative time, an opportunity for reflection and observation which finds its way into your music now?

Tamara: Yeah, absolutely. I think the one good thing about growing up in a rural place is you have so much time to yourself, and so it gives you this gift of time, perhaps, and patience, maybe.

Lauren: You’re also an actor. Would you say that your work as an actor growing up was another way to observe and explore the lives of other people?

Tamara: Yeah, it really was. I only started acting as a teenager, and I mostly acted as a teenager and into my early to mid-20s. It was really interesting because as a teenager I was extremely shy and couldn’t figure out the social structure of my school, which is part of why I wound up acting. I was like, ‘I’ve got to get out of here somehow,’ and my parents were like, ‘This seems like a good idea.’ Acting was really good for me because it allowed me to just be someone else and then I could hide, which was a really useful way to get through that part of life for me. As I got older, it took me a long time to figure out how to be myself in the world, but I did figure it out.

Lauren: In your life and work there have been times of isolation and introspection, but you also seek collaborative creative projects. You were a member of the Toronto musical collective Bruce Peninsula, alongside Taylor Kirk from Timber Timbre and others. What is it about the collaborative aspect of songwriting that appeals to you?

Tamara: It’s really interesting because when I first got into music in my early 20s, when I was living in Toronto, that was something that was so exciting about it. The moment I met musicians, I just felt like, ‘Ah, these are my people. I understand how to be.’ I really love touring. Touring is literally spending your life with several other people in very close quarters. There’s this beautiful intimacy to it that you don’t get in a normal job. Even though I am an introspective person, I spend a lot of time alone, I think it’s something that’s really special and something that I value in music.

Simon: You worked closely with Daniel Romano and released the project Duets together. I’m not sure ‘cowboy’ is the right word from the interview I read, but you’ve described him as someone who picks up an instrument, tests an idea and throws it away if it’s not immediately working. There’s a real fast pace to that style. How did you find your methods interacted in the studio?

Tamara: Daniel was a really formative person for me to meet because I was a very studious person. Even though the first music I made was pretty wild, as I got further into it I couldn’t help but want to do the right thing. I wanted to do everything right and do a good job. I’m that kind of person. I’m really glad I met Dan when I did because he’s the opposite of that. He doesn’t care. He’s like, ‘This is good, this is bad.’ He has very clear opinions. I just realised from working with him how important it is in music to not try to do the right thing. The more that you’re trying to do what you think you should do, the worse your music is going to be. Dan really taught me that, so I’m grateful to him for teaching me that.

Simon: You’ve said music is a beautiful and simple way to talk to people, that your songs are an invitation to conversation, sharing your experiences and exploring other people’s perspectives. How does the self-titled album reflect your own experiences and responses to the world over the past couple of years?

Tamara: Oh, man. There’s so much in this album. It’s such a kind of rambling monster of an album. There’s a lot in there. I wouldn’t even know where to start. But for sure, music to me is such a personal space because, like a lot of people, I listen to a lot of music on headphones, so it’s a solitary experience. To me, music from when I was young is this space where you can express things that you haven’t heard otherwise. I would hear a song and be like, ‘Ah, this is what this feels like,’ or, ‘I understand that this person has shared this experience with me.’ But had I met the person who wrote the song, we would never have discussed that. To me it’s such a special space to share these unusual things. When I put out this record there were people in my life who were like, ‘I had no idea you felt this way or this happened.’ These are the things I put in songs, not in conversations.

Lauren: You’ve said sometimes you’re writing from a perspective of fearlessness, even when you’re feeling the fear. Can you expand on that? How does writing allow you to explore contradictions like this?

Tamara: Yeah, I’ve thought a lot about that because I feel like classic songwriting and pop music has always been this space of people expressing fantasy or very simple ideas, like, ‘I will always love you,’ or something like this. What makes me excited about a song is trying to approach something that I haven’t heard in a song, or trying to express several angles of something. The song that I’ll play now, ‘Free’, is this weird interrogation of this idea of someone telling me that I can do anything I want, but me feeling like I can’t, but also realising that I can at the same time. It’s trying to write about all those angles in just a few verses.
